reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it primarily provides recruitment information for a Technical Support Associate position alongside an IBM-branded careers listing and application interface. The fraud-related caution is presented as a warning about purported IBM communications, not as a solicitation of money or credentials. Although the transcript includes a contradictory payment statement, it also says there are no fees, and the records do not establish a payment request, recipient, or completed transaction.

citations.quote: a private job information, recruitment has come out from IBM
The post name is technical support associate.
you'll have to click on the link here to apply.

opening.argument: The video links access to an IBM-branded job opportunity with an explicit payment statement and an application action. It says, "So you will have to pay for this," then directs viewers to click a link to apply. That is the core structure of a low-barrier acquisition scheme: viewers are encouraged to pursue a job while being told that payment is part of obtaining it. The later no-fee wording does not erase the earlier condition; it creates precisely the kind of contradiction that can leave applicants unsure whether money is required at some stage. The visible application flow reinforces that viewers are being moved toward participation rather than merely given neutral information.

citations.quote: So you will have to pay for this.
you'll have to click on the link here to apply.

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling the content recruitment information does not answer the payment-linked solicitation. The transcript expressly says applicants will have to pay before also saying there are no fees; that contradiction is not proof of a harmless warning. The application interface and "APPLY NOW" flow show viewers being directed into the opportunity, while the record does not identify when, why, or to whom payment would be made.

citations.quote: So you will have to pay for this.
And no fees. And you do not have to pay.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The argument treats an isolated contradictory sentence as an actual payment condition, but the same speaker states, "And no fees. And you do not have to pay." Nothing supplied identifies a fee, recipient, payment mechanism, or completed transaction. The IBM page and application controls show an ordinary job listing, and directing viewers to apply does not establish that money is exchanged.

citations.quote: And no fees. And you do not have to pay.

opening.argument: Several genuine risk signals appear together: an external application path, a Telegram contact link, and inconsistent claims about whether applicants must pay. The description supplies both an IBM careers URL and a Telegram link, while the narration says, "So you will have to pay for this" and later denies any fee. The IBM-branded page also displays fraud-related warnings about purported IBM communications. Taken together, this is not simply a clean job announcement: viewers are exposed to an off-platform contact route, an unresolved money condition, and an identity context in which fraudulent offers are specifically relevant. A careful viewer would have reason to treat the opportunity as a scam risk rather than rely on the branding alone.

citations.quote: Official Notification : https://careers.ibm.com/ShowJob/Id/645242/Technical%20Support%20Associate Telegram Link : https://t.me/getjobupdate
So you will have to pay for this.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense relies on IBM branding, but branding is exactly what a deceptive recruitment pitch could invoke, and the supplied page itself contains fraud-related warnings. The Telegram link is an additional external contact route, not evidence of a controlled IBM application process. Most importantly, the defense cannot resolve the narration's direct payment statement merely by selecting the later denial.

citations.quote: Telegram Link : https://t.me/getjobupdate
So you will have to pay for this.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: These are risk indicators, not proof of a scam transaction. The description labels the IBM URL as an official notification and separately provides a Telegram link, but it does not say Telegram is required for applying or that payment occurs there. The page's fraud warning supports caution, while the narration explicitly says, "And no fees. And you do not have to pay." No supplied evidence shows a fee, credential request, or deceptive outcome.

And no fees. And you do not have to pay.

opening.argument: Although presented as job information, the video functions as a recruitment promotion that steers viewers toward participation. It identifies the IBM Technical Support Associate role, says freshers can apply, directs viewers to click the link, and ends by inviting questions and subscriptions. The description adds a Telegram route alongside the purported official notification. That combination turns the content from detached reporting into an actionable funnel for applicants. Because the narration also includes the unexplained claim that viewers must pay, the promotional framing makes the opportunity materially risky: it encourages people to proceed before the financial condition is clarified.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The fact that the video names a job and tells viewers how to apply does not make it neutral reporting; it is plainly urging participation. The narration says viewers can apply and directs them to click, while the description provides Telegram contact. The defense's reference to an application page therefore confirms the steering behavior rather than disproving it. A promotional job funnel with an unexplained payment statement warrants the scam characterization.

The argument overreads a likely transcription error or contradiction: the same narration says, "And no fees. And you do not have to pay." The IBM careers page visibly presents a Technical Support Associate listing and application controls, but the supplied material does not show that applicants were charged or that the Telegram route was mandatory.
